newsitem.title: USA: Administration watches EU closely on Boeing merger.
newsitem.headline: Administration watches EU closely on Boeing merger.

text.p: The Clinton administration, spurred by a bipartisan group of senators, warned on Monday that it was watching the European Union closely to be sure it weighs the merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. objectively.

"We have made it clear to EU officials that it is essential that extraneous factors play no role in the commission's competition analysis of this merger and that we are watching that process closely," an administration official said.

Later, Sen. Slade Gorton, R.-Wash. -- author of a letter sent Friday to President Clinton week on the issue -- said U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky assured him in a meeting Monday the merger "is of intense interest and concern to the administration."
"It was a pretty good answer," he said.
Like the United States, Europe has an authority that reviews business combinations for their effect on competition.

The European Union is reviewing the merger because Boeing does a brisk business with European airlines. It has authority to impose a fine equal to 10 percent of Boeing's annual gross world income if it decides the merger is anti-competitive.

Boeing and McDonnell Douglas late last year announced their merger, which would narrow the number of American producers of large passenger jets from two to one. That has raised questions in Europe about the effect on the European consortium manufacturing airliners, Airbus Industrie.
In Brussels, a source close to the competition minister said Monday the merger investigation was being conducted objectively.
A bipartisan group of seven senators, most of them from states where Boeing has large plants, have signed a letter to President Clinton accusing the EU of prejudging the matter.

Americans and Europeans have been negotiating over concerns that each is subsidising its own commercial airline industry. Some American officials believe the Europeans are angling to use the Boeing merger to increase subsidies to Airbus.
But the Europeans said Monday that there was no link between the subsidy talks and the review by competition officials, which are conducted by two separate ministries.

"We have not established any link between the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas case and Airbus and between the merger and the discussions on subsidies," said a source close to the EU competition minister in Brussels.
Last month, EU Competititon Minister Karel Van Miert said the commission might act against the merger because of competitive concerns.

"I can't see how possibly we can give our authorisation to the merger with such a system in place," he told Reuters during a visit to Washington last month. "Now, it would not be good enough to bless the merger, that must be clear as well."
The group of senators signing the letter labeled Van Miert's statements "inappropriate," "prejudicial" and "troubling," and said they do "grave harm" to due process.
The letter was signed by the senators from Kansas, Missouri and Washington states. It was also signed by Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican.
Speaking briefly with a reporter as she left Gorton's office Monday, Barshefsky was asked if she believed the EU was objectively reviewing the Boeing deal.
"I have no way of judging that," she said as she walked toward an elevator.
